We present an x-ray spectromicroscopic investigation of single-crystalline magnetic FeMn/Co bilayers on Cu(001), using X-ray magnetic circular (XMCD) and linear (XMLD) dichroism at the Co and Fe L3 absorption edges in combination with photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM). Using the magnetic coupling between the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer we are able to produce magnetic domains with two different crystallographic orientations of the magnetic easy axis within the same sample at the same time. We find a huge difference in the XMLD contrast between the two types of magnetic domains, which we discuss in terms of intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of XMLD of the Co layer. We also demonstrate that due to the high sensitivity of the method, the small number of induced ferromagnetic Fe moments at the FeMn-Co interface is sufficient to obtain magnetic contrast from XMLD in a metallic system.

# Investigation of Magnetic Coupling in FeMn/Co Bilayers

## Overview

This study investigates single-crystalline magnetic FeMn/Co bilayers grown on a Cu(001) substrate. The magnetic properties of these bilayers were examined using a powerful combination of X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD), integrated with photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM). This experimental approach enables spatially resolved imaging of magnetic domains while simultaneously providing element-specific magnetic information.

## Controlling Magnetic Domain Orientation

A central achievement of this work lies in the ability to exploit the magnetic coupling between the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer. Through this interfacial coupling, the researchers were able to produce magnetic domains exhibiting two distinct crystallographic orientations of the magnetic easy axis within the same sample simultaneously. This controlled coexistence of differently oriented domains provides an ideal platform for comparative studies of magnetic anisotropy effects.

## Observation of XMLD Contrast

A key finding of the investigation was the observation of a large difference in XMLD contrast between the two types of magnetic domains. This pronounced contrast difference is attributed to the intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of XMLD in the Co layer. The dependence of the XMLD signal on the crystallographic orientation of the magnetic easy axis highlights the sensitivity of linear dichroism to the underlying crystal symmetry and the local magnetic structure.

## Sensitivity of the Method

The high sensitivity of this experimental method is particularly noteworthy. It allows the detection of magnetic contrast originating from the small number of induced ferromagnetic Fe moments located at the FeMn–Co interface. The capability to resolve such subtle magnetic signals via XMLD in a metallic system demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique for probing interfacial magnetism, where only a limited number of magnetic moments contribute to the measurable signal.

# X-ray Dichroism Study of Single-Crystalline FeMn/Co Bilayers on Cu(001)

## Introduction

The interaction between ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM) materials at their shared interface underlies many phenomena of central importance to modern spintronics, most notably exchange bias and interfacial exchange coupling. Understanding and controlling the magnetic order in such systems requires experimental techniques capable of resolving both the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic spin arrangements with high spatial resolution and elemental specificity. In this work, we investigated single-crystalline FeMn/Co bilayers grown epitaxially on a Cu(001) substrate, using a combination of X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) in conjunction with photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM). This approach allows the simultaneous imaging of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic domains while retaining sensitivity to the individual chemical elements involved.

## Concept and Methodology

The key idea of our experiment was to exploit the coupling between the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer to engineer magnetic domains with well-defined crystallographic properties. Because the direction of the ferromagnetic magnetization is transferred to the antiferromagnet through interfacial exchange coupling, we were able to create, within a single sample, domains characterized by two distinct crystallographic easy-axis orientations. This configuration provides an ideal testbed for probing the intrinsic magnetic response of the system, since the two domain types differ in their orientation relative to the crystal lattice while sharing the same chemical composition and structure.

XMCD, which is sensitive to the projection of the magnetic moment along the X-ray helicity, was used to map the ferromagnetic domain structure of the Co layer. XMLD, which responds to the axis rather than the direction of the magnetic moment and is therefore suited to antiferromagnets, was employed to probe the spin arrangement in the FeMn layer as well as the induced moments at the interface. The PEEM technique provided the spatial resolution necessary to correlate the magnetic contrast with the underlying domain configuration.

## Results

Our measurements revealed a pronounced difference in the XMLD contrast between the two types of domains. This large contrast difference cannot be explained solely by the orientation of the antiferromagnetic spin axis relative to the X-ray polarization; instead, we attribute it primarily to the intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of the system. The XMLD signal thus reflects the coupling between the magnetic moments and the crystallographic axes, providing direct evidence that the observed contrast is governed by the anisotropic electronic and magnetic structure of the material rather than by geometry alone.

Furthermore, we demonstrated that the sensitivity of the combined XMLD-PEEM method is sufficient to detect magnetic contrast even from the comparatively small number of ferromagnetically induced Fe moments located at the metallic FeMn–Co interface. These induced moments, arising from the proximity of the ferromagnetic Co layer, represent only a small fraction of the total magnetic signal, yet they could be resolved clearly in our measurements. This highlights the exceptional sensitivity of the technique to weak interfacial magnetic effects.

## Conclusions

In summary, our study establishes single-crystalline FeMn/Co bilayers on Cu(001) as a model system for exploring the interplay between ferromagnetic–antiferromagnetic coupling and magneto-crystalline anisotropy. By engineering domains with different easy-axis orientations, we were able to isolate and quantify the intrinsic contribution to the XMLD contrast. The demonstrated ability to detect the small induced Fe moments at the metallic interface underscores the power of combining X-ray dichroism techniques with photoelectron emission microscopy for the investigation of subtle interfacial magnetic phenomena, opening the way to more detailed studies of exchange coupling in epitaxial spintronic systems.

# Investigating FeMn Antiferromagnets with XMCD and XMLD

## Introduction

Antiferromagnetic materials play a central role in modern spintronics, particularly in the development of exchange-biased devices such as spin valves and magnetic tunnel junctions. Among these materials, the iron-manganese alloy (FeMn) has attracted significant attention due to its robust antiferromagnetic ordering and its widespread use as a pinning layer in magnetic multilayers. Understanding the magnetic structure of FeMn requires advanced characterization techniques, and two synchrotron-based methods—X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism (XMLD)—have proven especially valuable.

## FeMn as an Antiferromagnetic Material

FeMn in its γ-phase (face-centered cubic) is an antiferromagnet with a Néel temperature that depends on composition, typically ranging near room temperature for the equiatomic alloy. Its ability to establish exchange bias when coupled to a ferromagnetic layer makes it technologically important. However, because antiferromagnets possess no net macroscopic magnetization, conventional magnetometry cannot easily probe their internal spin arrangement. This is where element-specific X-ray spectroscopy becomes indispensable.

## X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD)

XMCD measures the difference in absorption of left- and right-circularly polarized X-rays as they pass through a magnetic material. This effect is sensitive to the **net magnetic moment** projected along the photon propagation direction. Key features of XMCD include:

- **Element specificity**: By tuning the X-ray energy to the absorption edges (e.g., the Fe and Mn L₂,₃ edges), the magnetic contributions of individual elements can be isolated.
- **Quantitative analysis**: Through sum rules, XMCD allows separate determination of spin and orbital magnetic moments.
- **Ferromagnetic sensitivity**: Because it responds to net magnetization, XMCD is ideal for studying the ferromagnetic layer and any uncompensated interfacial moments in FeMn-based systems.

In exchange-bias studies, XMCD can reveal small uncompensated spins at the FeMn interface that are believed to be responsible for the pinning effect.

## X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism (XMLD)

XMLD, by contrast, measures the difference in absorption of linearly polarized X-rays oriented parallel versus perpendicular to the magnetic axis. Crucially, XMLD depends on the **square of the magnetization** (⟨M²⟩), making it sensitive to the orientation of spin axes regardless of their sign. This property makes XMLD uniquely suited for antiferromagnets:

- **Antiferromagnetic order parameter**: XMLD can directly probe the spin-axis orientation in FeMn, even though the net magnetization is zero.
- **Domain imaging**: When combined with photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM), XMLD enables visualization of antiferromagnetic domain structures.
- **Interface coupling**: XMLD helps map how the antiferromagnetic spin axis in FeMn aligns relative to the ferromagnetic layer, providing insight into the microscopic origin of exchange bias.

## Complementary Use of XMCD and XMLD

The two techniques provide complementary information. XMCD reveals the ferromagnetic and uncompensated moments, while XMLD reveals the underlying antiferromagnetic spin structure. By combining both measurements on FeMn-based heterostructures, researchers can construct a comprehensive picture of the interfacial magnetic configuration:

| Technique | Polarization | Sensitivity | Ideal for |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|-----------|
| XMCD | Circular | Net magnetization (⟨M⟩) | Ferromagnets, uncompensated spins |
| XMLD | Linear | Spin-axis orientation (⟨M²⟩) | Antiferromagnets, spin axes |

## Conclusion

The study of FeMn antiferromagnets exemplifies the power of polarization-dependent X-ray absorption spectroscopy. XMCD and XMLD together allow researchers to disentangle the complex magnetic interactions at ferromagnet/antiferromagnet interfaces, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying exchange bias. As spintronic devices continue to advance—particularly in the emerging field of antiferromagnetic spintronics—these element-specific, symmetry-sensitive techniques will remain essential tools for probing and engineering magnetic order at the nanoscale.

# X-ray Magnetic Dichroism Studies of Antiferromagnetic-Ferromagnetic Coupling in Thin Film Heterostructures

## Abstract

The magnetic coupling between antiferromagnetic (AFM) and ferromagnetic (FM) layers underpins the exchange bias phenomenon central to spintronic device functionality, yet element-specific and interface-sensitive characterization of the underlying spin structures remains challenging. Here we employ complementary X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism (XMLD) spectroscopy to probe the coupled magnetic order in prototypical AFM/FM thin film systems, including CoO/Fe and NiO/Co bilayers grown by molecular beam epitaxy. By tuning the photon energy to the relevant L-edge absorption resonances, we achieve simultaneous, element-resolved measurement of the ferromagnetic net moment (via XMCD) and the antiferromagnetic axis orientation (via XMLD), enabling direct correlation of interfacial spin configurations across the AFM-FM boundary.

Temperature-dependent measurements through the Néel transition reveal a systematic reorientation of the antiferromagnetic spin axis that tracks the ferromagnetic magnetization direction, providing direct spectroscopic evidence of interfacial exchange coupling. Angular-dependent XMLD analysis quantifies the relationship between the AFM easy axis and the FM magnetization, demonstrating both collinear and orthogonal coupling geometries depending on interface crystallography and layer thickness. Field-cooling protocols establish a correlation between the frozen interfacial uncompensated moments detected by XMCD and the macroscopic exchange bias field measured via magnetometry. We further resolve a fraction of pinned, rotatable spins at the interface that governs the coercivity enhancement and training effects.

These results establish combined XMCD/XMLD as a powerful methodology for disentangling the interfacial spin structure responsible for exchange bias, offering critical insight for the rational design of antiferromagnetic spintronic devices. The demonstrated sensitivity to buried interface magnetism provides a pathway toward understanding emergent phenomena in complex oxide and metallic AFM/FM heterostructures.

---

*Keywords: exchange bias, X-ray magnetic dichroism, antiferromagnetism, interfacial coupling, spintronics, synchrotron spectroscopy*

# Abstract

Magneto-crystalline anisotropy plays a pivotal role in determining the magnetic domain configuration and spin orientation in single-crystalline metallic systems, yet its influence on X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) contrast remains incompletely understood. Here, we present a systematic investigation of the interplay between magneto-crystalline anisotropy and XMLD contrast in epitaxially grown single-crystalline metallic magnetic bilayers. Using element-specific photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM) combined with angular-dependent XMLD measurements, we disentangle the crystalline and magnetic contributions to the observed dichroic signal across a series of bilayer heterostructures with controlled crystallographic orientations. Our results demonstrate that the XMLD contrast exhibits a pronounced dependence on the relative orientation between the X-ray polarization vector, the crystallographic axes, and the local magnetization direction, revealing a non-trivial angular signature that deviates from the idealized quadratic dependence predicted for polycrystalline references. By varying the layer thickness and interfacial coupling strength, we further establish how magneto-crystalline anisotropy energy landscapes govern the domain structure and, consequently, modulate the magnitude and sign of the XMLD contrast at each constituent layer. Quantitative analysis, supported by atomic multiplet and ligand-field calculations, allows us to separate the intrinsic crystal-field-induced anisotropy of the XMLD tensor from magnetization-driven effects. These findings provide a robust framework for the correct interpretation of XMLD imaging in crystalline metallic systems and offer critical guidance for the design of anisotropy-engineered spintronic devices where accurate magnetic contrast quantification is essential.

---

*Keywords:* X-ray magnetic linear dichroism, magneto-crystalline anisotropy, single-crystalline bilayers, PEEM, spintronics, magnetic domain imaging
